thread.title: Intel Earnings Suffer From iPhone Softness, Cloud Slowdown

author: Ashraf Eassa, The Motley Fool
title: Intel Earnings Suffer From iPhone Softness, Cloud Slowdown
text:
On Jan. 24, chip giant Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) reported its financial results for the fourth quarter of 2018 and issued initial guidance for 2019. I'll cut right to the chase -- Intel's results were underwhelming. Full-year 2018 revenue came in at $70.8 billion, which was $400 million lower than the company's own guidance issued when it reported its third-quarter results back on Oct. 25, 2018 -- although revenue was up 13% from 2017 levels. The company also issued new guidance for full-year 2019 revenue of $71.5 billion -- up just slightly from what it delivered in 2018.
In 2018, Intel's earnings per share (EPS) came in at $4.58 on a non- GAAP basis, which was a whopping 32% improvement from 2017 levels. The company's EPS outlook for 2019, however, is $4.60, representing growth of less than half a percent.
A wafer of Intel Xeon server processors with packaged versions of those chips in front of the wafer. More Image source: Intel.
Let's take a closer look at what drove the results and guidance.
Intel had an iPhone problem Intel is a supplier of cellular modems for Apple 's (NASDAQ: AAPL) current iPhone offerings and the exclusive supplier of modems for Apple's freshest products: the iPhone XR, iPhone XS, and iPhone XS Max. A key factor in Intel's miss relative to expectations derived from weakness in modem sales. It's no secret that iPhone demand is proving disappointing, something that Apple confirmed when it issued a revenue warning on Jan. 2 . Intel says that fourth-quarter modem revenue was roughly $200 million below its expectations, which accounts for about half of the $400 million total top-line miss.
Nevertheless, while the modem business did fall short compared to guidance, it's worth noting that the company's modem revenue was still up a solid 68% from the same quarter a year ago, as Intel went from being one of two modem suppliers in Apple's flagship iPhones to the sole vendor.
Data center miss accounted for the rest Back in October, Intel told investors that it expected its data center group (DCG) revenue to hit $6.3 billion in the fourth quarter of 2018. The company missed that guidance, raking in revenue of just $6.1 billion -- $200 million below expectations. This accounts for the remainder of the full-year revenue miss for 2018.
The company blamed the lower-than-expected DCG revenue on "softer China demand & cloud deceleration."
Digging deeper into the results, DCG saw revenue from cloud service providers grow 24% year over year, revenue from communications service providers rise 12%, and revenue from its enterprise and government segment -- which started the year in weak shape but perked up over the course of 2018 -- decline 5%.
Inside the 2019 guidance miss Analysts had expected Intel to guide for 2019 revenue of $73.25 billion and EPS of $4.55. The revenue expectations, unfortunately, turned out to be overly optimistic to the tune of nearly $2 billion, although the company forecasts EPS of $4.60, which is slightly above consensus.
In its earnings presentation, Intel provided a reconciliation between its view of 2019 from back in October and what it's thinking is now. While the company's capital expenditure (CapEx), tax rate, and gross margin expectations are approximately "consistent with [Intel's] October assessment," its view of operating margin deteriorated from about flat relative to 2018 to down less than a percentage point.
